deep.reconstruction:
Context (pp. 3-4). Grothendieck is axiomatizing a category M of 'models' (cell shapes). Each model of dimension n is given by a finite poset J_n with a greatest element d_n, and J_n^* := J_n \ {d_n}. He lists three examples.
- Ex 1 (simplices): J_n is the poset of non-empty faces of Δ_n, of cardinality 2^{n+1}-1.
- Ex 2 (pinned cubes): J_n is the poset of faces of the n-cube, of cardinality 3^n.
- Ex 3 (hemispheres): J_n = (Δ_{n-1} × {±1}) ∐ {d_n}, with {±1} carrying the chaotic order. This is the cell poset of the hemispherical CW structure on the n-disk, of cardinality 2n+1. It is the globular shape.
The common property (a) from the previous page: |J_n^*| is an (n-1)-sphere and |J_n| is an n-disk.

This page adds property (b): the posets I_n^* (= J_n^*), viewed as boundary complexes of polyhedra, are regular. That is, Aut(I_n^*) acts transitively on flags, the maximal chains ξ_0 < ξ_1 < ... < ξ_{n-1}.

He then asks for other sequences of posets (P_n)_{n≥1}, with P_n = I_{n+1}^*, such that:
- (a) P_n is the face poset of a regular spherical polytope (a regular cellulation of S^n);
- (b) for every ξ in P_n, the lower interval (P_n)_{≤ξ} is isomorphic to some P_{n'} with n' ≤ n (strictly, to the closed cell poset of the matching lower-dimensional member).
He guesses this 'must be in Coxeter's books'. The margin asks whether b) follows from a). He adds that he would above all like to be able to find such families satisfying the transitivity condition.

Purpose: to find all 'regular' shape categories analogous to Δ, the cubes and the globes. Next page: the full subcategory B_0 of presheaves that are unions of model subobjects, with 'M-pinnings' (length maps τ_K and admissible maps J_n → K).

Answer to his question in modern terms. A flag-transitive spherical (abstract) regular polytope of rank n+1 is the universal polytope with Schläfli symbol {p_1,...,p_n}, with finite string Coxeter group. All its k-faces are isomorphic to the regular polytope {p_1,...,p_{k-1}}.
- So given a), condition b) reduces to 'facet(P_n) ≅ P_{n-1}'. Hence the family is encoded by one infinite sequence p_1, p_2, ... whose every truncation gives a finite Coxeter group.
- Classification. The linear diagram splits at the 2's into finite components: A_m, B_m (4 at an end), F_4, H_3, H_4, I_2(p).
- Non-degenerate families (all p_i ≥ 3, genuine convex polytopes) are exactly two: simplices {3,3,...} and cubes {4,3,3,...}. Cross-polytopes fail because their facets are simplices. The 24-cell, 120-cell and 600-cell families stop in dimension 4.
- Allowing p_i = 2 (digons, as in Ex 3) gives many more: {2,2,2,...} (the hemispheres/globes); {p,2,2,...}; {3,2,3,2,...} (join-type); {3,3,2,4,3,3,...}; and so on. A '2' acts as a join/suspension-type operation.
- So the answer to the margin question is no: a) alone does not force b), since one needs the coherence facet(P_n) = P_{n-1}.
errors: The flag is written ξ_0 < ξ_1 < ... ≤ ξ_{n-1}; it should be strict throughout.

Calling all three examples convex polyhedra is inaccurate: the hemispherical example (Schläfli {2,2,...}) has digon faces and is not the face lattice of a convex polytope. It is only a regular CW decomposition of the sphere (an abstract regular polytope).

The margin question 'is b) a consequence of a)?' has answer no in general. Regularity forces all k-faces of P_n to be mutually isomorphic and regular, but not that they belong to the given sequence; that needs facet(P_n) ≅ P_{n-1}.

ideas.what: Simplices, cubes and hemispheres (globes) unified as sequences of posets J_n whose boundary realizes a sphere and whose lower intervals are again models
ideas.modern_name: regular cell shape categories / test-category-like shape categories (Δ, □, globular Θ_0-type)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck, Pursuing Stacks (1983) for the test-category viewpoint; Street, Batanin and others for globes
ideas.where_published: Pursuing Stacks discusses simplicial and cubical shapes and test categories; unsure whether the hemispherical poset appears there

ideas.what: Regularity as flag-transitivity of the automorphism group of the face poset
Question: classify sequences of regular spherical polytopes P_n whose lower intervals are earlier members of the sequence
ideas.modern_name: infinite Schläfli symbols with all truncations of spherical (finite Coxeter) type
ideas.usually_credited_to: follows from Coxeter's classification of finite Coxeter groups

missed.claim: Grothendieck asks which other 'regular' shape families exist besides simplices, cubes and hemispheres. The answer via Coxeter theory: among non-degenerate (convex) ones, only simplices and cubes. Admitting digons (p_i = 2) gives an infinite list of degenerate families, built by concatenating finite Coxeter components; the globular {2,2,...} is the simplest. Each would give a candidate shape category for homotopy types or higher categories.
missed.quote: Y a-t-il d'autres exemples d'une suite (P_n)_{n≥1} d'ens. ordonnés ... a) P_n est un polyèdre régulier sphérique b) ... (P_n)_{≤ξ} ≃ P_{n'} ... (Ça doit être dans les livres de Coxeter!)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This links shape categories for higher category theory (simplicial, cubical, globular) to Coxeter/Schläfli classification. That link is rarely made explicit. It suggests exotic 'regular' shape categories (e.g. built from {3,2,3,2,...}) whose test-category or model-structure properties seem not to have been studied.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This gives a Coxeter-theoretic reason why exactly simplices, cubes and globes recur as shape categories. Literature comparing these shapes usually does not phrase the comparison via flag-transitive polytopes.

deep.surprise_reason: A natural, open-ended question placing simplices, cubes and globes in a single regular-polytope framework, answerable by Coxeter classification. The individual ideas are classical, but the explicit Coxeter-group angle on shape categories is not standard. The question is left unfinished on the page.
transcription_corrections: 'réalisés comme (demi) polyèdres [?] convexes [?]' is more likely 'réalisés comme (bords?) polyèdres convexes' (the boundary of the polyhedron); uncertain.
The flag should read 'ξ_0 < ξ_1 < ... < ξ_{n-1}' (the first symbol was corrected from a crossed-out one).
'pour [?] ces propriétés' plausibly reads 'jouissant de ces propriétés' or similar.
'P_{n-1}' written under the crossed-out '(I_n^*)_{n∈N, n≥1}' appears to be an indexing remark consistent with the margin note 'P_n = I_{n+1}^*'.
